strengths: Well-motivated framework: Using Multi-Codebook Vector Quantization (MVQ) to convert continuous representations of speech and audio teachers into discrete tokens successfully bridges the domain gap. It avoids the representation collapse or destructive interference typically associated with direct continuous feature-matching losses in disparate domains.

Excellent experimental results: SPEAR sets a new state-of-the-art on the SUPERB benchmark, outperforming WavLM Large on 12 of 15 tasks. It also achieves highly competitive results on the HEAR benchmark, demonstrating outstanding versatility across both speech and general audio tasks.

Novel and effective auxiliary techniques: The asymmetrical training loss strategy and the token mixing mechanism (which probabilistically combines targets from mixed audio sources) are solid, well-designed contributions that show clear, measurable gains in complex sound scenes.

Thorough and well-structured ablation studies: The paper provides extensive analysis, including comparative visualizations of MVQ vs. k-means feature spaces, studies on the number of codebooks, layer selection, and a rigorous controlled comparison with the USAD baseline under identical data budgets.
weaknesses: Multi-stage pipeline complexity: The training process requires pre-training the MVQ quantizers on frozen teacher representations before student pre-training can begin. This makes the overall workflow more complex than end-to-end self-supervised frameworks.

Heavy reliance on large-scale teacher models: The quality of the learned representations is structurally bound to the initial teacher models (WavLM and Dasheng), meaning performance and domain reach are primarily constrained by the availability of high-quality external teachers.

Minor performance trade-offs: The dual-domain models still experience minor performance trade-offs on specific specialized tasks compared to their single-domain specialist counterparts, although scaling the model to the XLarge size partially alleviates this.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: learning a unified self-supervised representation space that performs well on both speech-centric tasks (requiring high-level semantics) and general audio tasks (requiring fine-grained acoustic detail).

SPEAR achieves state-of-the-art performance across major benchmarks, outperforming WavLM Large on 12 of 15 tasks on SUPERB and delivering highly competitive results on the HEAR benchmark, surpassing other unified models like USAD.

The evaluation is thorough, including downstream fine-tuning on ASR and Audio Tagging as well as frozen representation evaluations. The paper also includes extensive ablation studies in the appendix covering tokenizers (MVQ vs. k-means), number of codebooks, loss weighting, and teacher models.
The proposed token mixing mechanism is a simple yet effective way to handle overlapping sources, showing clear improvements on source separation and enhancement tasks.
weaknesses: The framework relies heavily on pre-trained domain-specific expert teachers (WavLM and Dasheng). This means the performance of SPEAR is upper-bounded or guided closely by the quality of these teachers, making it more of a multi-teacher distillation framework rather than a pure bottom-up self-supervised method.

The pre-training pipeline is complex and computationally expensive. It requires first training (or obtaining) specialized teacher models, training separate MVQ quantizers, and then performing the joint masked-token pre-training with asymmetric objectives.
The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, as it combines existing ideas like Multi-codebook Vector Quantisation (MVQ), masked-token prediction (from HuBERT/wav2vec), and teacher distillation.

The justification for the 'asymmetrical' pre-training strategy—where speech tokens are predicted for general audio but audio tokens are not predicted for speech—is mostly empirical. A deeper theoretical or intuitive explanation of why predicting speech tokens on environmental audio acts as a good regularizer would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical performance: SPEAR achieves a new state-of-the-art on the SUPERB benchmark (outperforming WavLM Large on 12 of 15 tasks) and exhibits highly competitive performance on the general audio HEAR benchmark.

Well-motivated unified design: Using Multi-codebook Vector Quantization (MVQ) to bridge speech (high-level semantics) and general audio (low-level acoustic features) is highly intuitive and successful, showing that fine-grained discrete tokens serve as a robust shared representation interface.

Comprehensive and rigorous ablation studies: The authors thoroughly investigate several key design decisions, including the number of codebooks, teacher layer selection, the dual-domain asymmetric loss, and a head-to-head controlled comparison with USAD.
Novel token mixing mechanism: Dynamically mixing supervision targets proportionally to their signal power is shown to successfully boost performance on source-separation and overlapping audio tasks.
weaknesses: Complex, multi-stage pre-training pipeline: SPEAR relies on pre-trained, frozen expert teachers (WavLM, Dasheng) and requires training separate MVQ quantizers before the actual student pre-training can begin. This makes the overall training pipeline highly dependent on external models.

Imbalanced pre-training data: The dual-domain models are trained on highly speech-dominated datasets (e.g., SA-197k contains only 13k hours of general audio). This limits general audio performance, as shown by the HEAR evaluation where SPEAR still trails behind Dasheng 1.2B in certain categories.

strengths: Strong Empirical Results: The proposed SPEAR framework shows state-of-the-art performance on the SUPERB benchmark, matching or outperforming the highly competitive WavLM Large. Additionally, in the joint speech-and-audio setting, SPEAR exhibits excellent versatility, bridging the performance across both SUPERB and HEAR benchmarks and outperforming prior joint distillation baselines.

Effective Unified representation strategy: Employing Multi-codebook Vector Quantisation (MVQ) to generate fine-grained targets effectively solves the problem of coarse-grained tokens (from k-means) being inadequate for general audio representation.

Thorough Ablation Studies: The authors provide an extensive set of experiments in Appendix G, validating key design choices including teacher selection, loss weight balancing, number of codebooks, and the choice of dual-domain training strategy.

Well-written and structured: The paper is organized clearly, progressing from single-domain settings to dual-domain joint training, making the contribution and benefits of the unified approach easy to follow.
weaknesses: Contradiction in Dual-Domain Strategy Description: There is a notable inconsistency between Equation 6 (Page 5) and the description of the ASYMMETRICAL strategy in Section G.5 (Page 24). Equation 6 indicates that the speech tokens $Z^s$ are computed universally (for both speech and audio inputs) while $Z^a$ is only computed when the input is general audio. However, Section G.5 states: 'For speech data, losses are computed against both $Z^s$ and $Z^a$. For audio data, loss is only computed against $Z^a$.' It appears the terms 'speech data' and 'audio data' were inadvertently swapped in the appendix description.

Heavy Dependency on Highly-Optimized Teachers: The framework relies entirely on pre-trained teachers (WavLM Large and Dasheng 1.2B) to extract continuous representations before quantizing them. This positions the proposed framework more as a discrete multi-teacher knowledge distillation pipeline rather than a fully self-contained SSL framework.

Incremental Methodological Novelty: While the application to unified speech and audio representation learning is successful, the core components of the system (MVQ, Zipformer, masked token prediction) are directly adopted from existing literature, limiting the conceptual novelty.

strengths: Successfully unifies speech and audio representation learning under a single token-based masked prediction framework, addressing a key challenge where different domains typically require distinct pre-training objectives.

Outstanding empirical performance: the speech-only model outperforms the highly competitive WavLM Large on 12 out of 15 SUPERB tasks, while the audio model achieves SOTA-level results on HEAR and AudioSet with fractionally less data.
Provides a thorough and well-structured set of ablation studies, evaluating the impact of teacher models, codebook sizes, loss formulations, and dual-domain training strategies.

Shows that non-hierarchical Multi-codebook Vector Quantization (MVQ) is highly effective for capturing fine-grained acoustic details necessary for general audio while retaining phonetic properties for speech.
weaknesses: High dependence on pre-trained teachers: The framework is essentially a masked distillation process requiring fully trained, highly optimized expert models (WavLM and Dasheng) to generate target tokens. This limits its applicability as a pure, first-principles self-supervised approach.

Asymmetrical dual-domain objective: The loss function is asymmetric, predicting speech tokens for general audio but not vice-versa, which is a heuristic designed to mitigate dataset imbalance rather than a clean, symmetric unification.

Limited fundamental architectural novelty: The core elements (Zipformer, MVQ, masked token prediction) are combined from existing works, meaning the contribution is primarily engineering-focused rather than introducing a new learning paradigm.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant challenge in auditory representation learning by proposing a unified self-supervised learning (SSL) framework, SPEAR, capable of jointly processing and representing both speech and general audio.

The performance of SPEAR is highly competitive. The speech-only version outperforms WavLM Large on 12 out of 15 SUPERB tasks, and the dual-domain SPEAR models maintain excellent performance across both SUPERB (speech) and HEAR (audio) benchmarks.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with a clear explanation of the methodology (MVQ, asymmetric dual-domain loss) and robust experimental details.

The authors provide comprehensive and insightful ablation studies covering teacher selection, codebook numbers, dual-domain training strategies, and target-reconstruction visualization, which strongly validate their design choices.
weaknesses: The framework is heavily reliant on existing strong teacher models (WavLM Large for speech and Dasheng 1.2B for audio) to generate the target representations. This means SPEAR behaves essentially as a multi-teacher knowledge distillation or feature-matching student model, rather than learning representations completely from scratch.

The dual-domain training corpus is highly imbalanced (84k hours of speech vs 13k hours of audio). Although the proposed asymmetrical loss mitigates this imbalance to some extent, the dual-domain model still suffers from performance degradation in some environment and music-related tasks on HEAR compared to the audio-only specialist.

The application of multi-codebook vector quantization (MVQ) to generate fine-grained targets is interesting, but multi-codebook designs (such as Residual Vector Quantization in EnCodec) are already widely used in audio/speech tokenization, making the core technical novelty somewhat incremental.
